output.title: Recovering from partial automation means one workflow, not the whole business
output.body:
If you are recovering from partial automation, do not start by asking, “What AI can we add back?” Start with one workflow that was partly automated, then stalled, broke, or was abandoned. Invoice data entry, lead follow-up, and customer FAQ replies are different problems; mixing them together is how small automations turn into maintenance chores.

The bounded decision is simple: keep investing only if the workflow is repeatable, measurable, and frequent enough to justify the setup work. That 8–10 hours-a-week pain point is only a persona example, not a benchmark or a promise. If the underlying process has changed, a broken automation may just need to stay broken.

One practical diagnostic question is: who approves the output? If the answer is always “me” or “a person,” AI-assisted automation may fit. If the answer is “nobody checks it,” or the system would run without review, you need explicit controls before you trust it. Human approval stays mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

Next, do the boring part on purpose: pick one half-broken workflow, write down in two sentences what still happens by hand and where the automation failed, then mark whether the output needs human approval. If you cannot answer that cleanly, the problem is scope, not software. We build inside the owner’s own tools and accounts, and finished code stays with the owner; that is our no-lock-in policy, not a magic trick.
